content: Bloating is one of the most frequently reported gastrointestinal complaints. Patients often describe it as a subjective sensation of excessive gas, which is not always objectively present. There are numerous non-functional causes of abdominal bloating and distension. However, primary functional abdominal distension (FABD) should be diagnosed as a distinct condition and does not overlap with other functional gastrointestinal disorders. According to the Rome IV diagnostic criteria, FABD may coexist with mild abdominal pain and/or minor alterations in bowel movements. Randomized controlled trials have demonstrated that FABD can be effectively managed with antispasmodic medications combined with peppermint oil. A stepwise approach is typically required for the management of FABD. This includes dietary interventions, modulation of the gut microbiome, and medical therapy. Causes The causes of abdominal bloating are diverse and should be addressed based on the underlying etiology. Diagnostic Approach The American College of Gastroenterology guidelines provide an algorithm for the diagnosis of abdominal bloating. Treatment The American College of Gastroenterology guidelines also outline an algorithm for the treatment of abdominal bloating. Recommended Practices (Dos) The use of probiotics has been shown to help reduce bloating. Antidepressants may alleviate symptoms of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), but their efficacy in reducing bloating specifically remains unclear. Hypnotherapy has been reported to be beneficial in reducing bloating symptoms. Bowel training and diaphragmatic breathing techniques have shown promise in managing bloating, although the supporting data is not definitive. Practices to Avoid (Don’ts) Artificial sweeteners containing sorbitol, mannitol, and xylitol should be avoided as they can exacerbate bloating. Medications such as anticholinergics, opiates, calcium channel blockers, and certain antidepressants should also be avoided due to their potential to worsen bloating. Certain carbohydrates, such as those found in baked beans (20%), wheat, oats, potatoes, and corn (7–10%), and white rice (1%), are poorly absorbed in the intestine. These can predispose individuals to bloating and should be avoided in patients with significant bloating complaints.
